KAFKA-21492: Fix task corruption for segmented stores without segments under EOS (#24204)

https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21492

A segmented store (window and session stores) keeps its changelog
offsets in its segments. Without a segment, `AbstractSegments#commit`
has nothing to write to and `AbstractSegments#committedOffset` returns
`null`, while opening the store has already created its directory.

Under exactly-once, `ProcessorStateManager#initializeStoreOffsets` then
treats the task as corrupted every time it is initialized on an instance
that has its task directory (after a restart, a rebalance, or a switch
between active and standby). The whole task is wiped and restored, and
the restore creates the same empty store directory again, so it repeats.
A corrupted active task also triggers a rebalance. A store has no
segment when it was never written.

This patch reports the offset of a segmented store without segments as
`OFFSET_UNKNOWN`, which is what a key-value store commits when it has no
offset and what `ProcessorStateManager` already accepts. There is no
local data in that state, so nothing can be uncommitted. A store that
has a segment but no offset still reports none, and its task is still
wiped.

`GlobalStateManagerImpl` reads the same offset for global stores and
would seek to the sentinel, so it now ignores it and restores from the
beginning.

Testing:
- `SegmentedStoreWithoutSegmentsTest` (new) covers the behaviour end to
end with `TopologyTestDriver`: a task whose window or session store left
its empty directory behind is initialized under exactly-once, and a
store with a segment and no offset is still treated as corrupted. The
store directory is created by hand because `TopologyTestDriver#close`
deletes the state directory.
- `KeyValueSegmentsTest` covers the changed method: no segments reports
`OFFSET_UNKNOWN`, a segment without offsets reports `null`.

KAFKA-21469: Shrink NamedCache dirty key set (#24189)

`NamedCache#flush` and `NamedCache#clear` reset the `dirtyKeys` set with
`LinkedHashSet#clear()`. `HashMap#clear()` sets every slot of its table
to null, and the table never shrinks. Thus each reset costs as much as
the largest number of dirty keys that the set ever held. After one flush
with many distinct dirty keys, every later flush of that cache pays for
the large table, for the life of the task. The table also stays on the
heap, and `statestore.cache.max.bytes` does not count it.

This change clears the set in place while its size matches the load, and
replaces the set when a flush has fewer than a quarter of the peak keys
since the last allocation. The flush also does this check when it has no
dirty keys, so an idle store releases the table. A replacement on every
flush is simpler, but at a high steady cardinality it allocates a large
table on each flush, which caused many more GC cycles in the benchmark.

In a JMH benchmark of the put/flush cycle, after a burst of 100k dirty
keys, the mean cost of each cycle drops by 43–75%. In a steady workload,
it is never more than 2% slower than the current code. KAFKA-21469
contains the full results.

KAFKA-14249: Make TLS idle expiry test deterministic (#22943)

## Summary

- Wait for the channel to be fully ready before testing idle connection
expiry.
- Remove the TLS 1.3-specific flaky-test override so the shared test
runs normally for TLS 1.3.

## Motivation

Fixes [KAFKA-14249](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-14249).

The idle-expiry test only waited for the TCP connection to reach
`CONNECTED`. With TLS 1.3, the first subsequent poll can still process
handshake I/O and refresh the selector's last-active timestamp. The test
then misses the expiry deadline and was marked flaky and excluded from
normal test execution.

Waiting for `READY` makes the test precondition match the behavior being
tested: no handshake work remains before the idle period starts. This
lets the TLS 1.3 variant run as a regular regression test.

## Validation

- Ran the TLS 1.3 selector suite with `testCloseOldestConnection`
included; it passed.
- Ran `SelectorTest`, `Tls12SelectorTest`, and `Tls13SelectorTest`; all
passed.
- Ran `./gradlew :clients:test --no-build-cache --console=plain`
successfully.
- Ran `git diff --check` successfully.

KAFKA-21372: Build TaskExecutionMetadata and PartitionGroup#nextRecord log messages lazily (#24174)

Follow-up to #23985 as suggested by @[person].

### The issue
`TaskExecutionMetadata#canProcessTask` (every task and every loop) and
`PartitionGroup#nextRecord` (every record) pay for log messages that are
almost never written.

### Why it happened
`canProcessTask` formats its message with `String.format` on every call
even though it is only logged at trace level or once every 120 s. The
multi-argument trace calls in `nextRecord` build a varargs array and box
their values even with trace off.

### The fix
- `canProcessTask` keeps the message as a `Supplier<String>` and calls
it only when it logs.
- The multi-argument trace calls in `nextRecord` are guarded by
`isTraceEnabled()`.
### Tests
- `TaskExecutionMetadataTest#shouldNotFormatLogMessageUntilItIsLogged`
and

`PartitionGroupTest#shouldNotBuildTraceLogArgumentsInNextRecordWhenTraceIsDisabled`:
both fail without the fix and pass with it.
- The full `streams:test` run passes.

KAFKA-21480: Report the end offset of a warm-up task with nothing to restore (#23991)

A standby task, and so a warm-up task, learns the end offset of a
changelog only from a restored batch. With nothing to restore -- an
empty changelog, or local state already at the end of an idle changelog
-- no batch ever arrives. The client then keeps reporting an end offset
of Long.MAX_VALUE for the task, which the broker reads as an unknown
lag. The warm-up task therefore never counts as caught up, and its
migration stayed stages forever, holding a warm-up slot.

When the restore consumer of a standby task reports a lag of 0 for a
changelog without a restore end offset, the changelog reader now also
records the end offset, as the last offset like a restored batch does:
-1 for an empty changelog.

For such a changelog, the reader now reports one past that last offset
as the end offset, like the restore end offset of an active task or of a
source-topic changelog. A negative end offset would otherwise be summed
into Long.MAX_VALUE, and reach custom assignors through the assignor
API. A fully restored standby task now reports a lag of 0 instead of -1
per changelog.

The changelog reader now restores only the changelogs it fetches in its
current state: those of active tasks while it restores active tasks,
those of standby tasks while it updates standby tasks, and in both cases
only for tasks that are not paused. It pauses all other restoring
changelogs before each poll. A standby changelog is therefore left
untouched while active tasks restore, so a standby task registered
meanwhile does not record an end offset from the lag of its paused
changelog. The reported offsets of a paused standby changelog keep their

KAFKA-21070: Fix task cleanup when state updater shutdown is interrupted (#23549)

When a thread is interrupted while waiting for task removal,
`shutdownStateUpdater()` exits before stopping the updater and closing
the remaining tasks. This can leave state stores and their resources
open.

This PR addresses the interrupted-shutdown issue in KAFKA-21070. The
separate issue where the updater discarded tasks during shutdown was
already addressed by KAFKA-20721.

This change continues cleanup after an interrupted removal wait. It
collects completed removal results and drains the tasks left in the
updater queues. Checking the futures is necessary because a task whose
removal completed after the interrupted wait is no longer in those
queues and can only be recovered through its future.

`DefaultStateUpdater.shutdown()` also retries interrupted joins within
the original timeout. The updater must stop before the caller closes its
remaining tasks to avoid accessing them concurrently.

An interruption alone does not cause shutdown to throw. Removal waits
remain interruptible. Once an interruption is observed, its status is
recorded and cleared so cleanup can continue. The calling thread's
interrupt status is restored in an outer finally block when shutdown
exits, including when cleanup throws. Leaving the status set during
cleanup would make the remaining steps fail early, such as closing the
thread producer or joining the task executor threads.

`StreamThread.run()` also clears the interrupt status when the run loop
exits, before the uncaught exception handler and the shutdown run, and
restores it once the shutdown completes. Otherwise an interrupt that
stops the thread makes the removal waits give up immediately, so the
tasks are closed dirty and their restore progress is lost, and with the
streams protocol a replacement thread cannot be created on the dying
thread. The `TaskManager` changes still handle an interrupt that arrives
while the thread is already shutting down.

KAFKA-21102, KAFKA-21176: Treat member, group and target assignment metadata tombstones as authoritative on replay (#23530)

Log compaction of `__consumer_offsets` can remove some of the tombstones
written when a group or a member is deleted and keep the others, in two
ways:

- The offset map of the cleaner can get full in the middle of the batch
holding the tombstones. The cleaner keeps every record after the last
one it mapped, so if the delete horizon of the batch has already passed,
it removes the first tombstones of the batch, along with the records
they deleted, and keeps the others. Every load of the partition then
sees the partial deletion until a later cleaning removes the rest.
- When the group coordinator loads the partition while a cleaning runs,
it can read a group's records from the uncleaned copy of an earlier
segment and its deletion from the cleaned copy of a later one, in which
the cleaner removed some of the tombstones.

The replay of member metadata, group metadata and target assignment
metadata tombstones required the other tombstones of the deletion to
have been replayed first and threw `IllegalStateException` otherwise,
failing the whole partition load.

This change treats those three tombstones as authoritative: replaying
one implies the missing ones, and the inconsistency is logged at debug
level instead. The checks are relaxed for every replay, not only during
a load, since the same methods replay the records that the coordinator
writes.

- `removeMember` also removes the member's target assignment.
- `removeGroup` also unsubscribes the group from `groupsByTopics` and
removes a share group's state partition metadata.
- The target assignment metadata tombstone clears any remaining
per-member target assignments.

classic group downgrade removes the group without replaying its member

KAFKA-21467: Classic to consumer group conversion fails when no protocol is selected or a member does not support it (#24187)

`ConsumerGroup.fromClassicGroup` parses every member's subscription with
the selected protocol of the classic group. When the group is in
PreparingRebalance and has no selected protocol yet, this throws
`NoSuchElementException`. When a member that does not support the
selected protocol has joined, this throws `IllegalArgumentException`.
Both are returned as UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR, which is fatal for the new
consumer that triggers the conversion during an online upgrade.

This patch parses the subscription of each member's first protocol
instead. All the protocols of a member carry the same subscription, and
the consumer group already parses the first protocol for every JoinGroup
of a classic member.

KAFKA-21450: TimelineHashMap iteration at a snapshot returns duplicate or missing entries (#24146)

After `SnapshotRegistry.revertToSnapshot`, iterating a `TimelineHashMap`
or a `TimelineHashSet` at the reverted snapshot, or at an older one,
returns the elements that the revert restored twice, and can skip an
element once one of them is overwritten or removed again. The group
coordinator reverts a failed write and reads at the last committed
offset, so until the next write is committed, ConsumerGroupDescribe,
ShareGroupDescribe, StreamsGroupDescribe, OffsetFetch for all the
partitions of a group and ListGroups can return a member, a partition or
a group twice, or miss one.

The revert applies the deltas of the snapshot but leaves them in it. For
a hash table, the delta holds the elements that the revert puts back in
the current table, and the iteration reads both. Removing or overwriting
one of them again adds it to the delta a second time. Adding an element
that is already in a `BaseHashTable` replaces it, but `baseAddOrReplace`
checks the load factor before it looks for the element, so the delta
table can double without gaining an element. Once it is larger than the
current table, the iterator skips elements. `TimelineObject`,
`TimelineInteger` and `TimelineLong` are not affected because their
delta holds the value at the snapshot, which is the current value after
the revert.

When `revertToSnapshot` or `deleteSnapshot(long)` deletes a snapshot,
`HashTier.mergeFrom` merges its tier into the tier of the previous
snapshot. It never clears the list of the slot it unpacks, so each slot
adds the elements of all the previous slots again. The merge then takes
time quadratic in the size of the tier, and the merged tier can grow
larger than the current table in the same way. A revert applies the
merged tier and, with this patch, drops it. `deleteSnapshot(long)`,
which no production code calls, keeps it, and iterating at the previous
snapshot can then skip elements.

KAFKA-20999: [2/N] Add rack-aware standby task assignment to sticky assignor (#23588)

Second part of rack-aware standby placement for streams groups. It wires
RackAwareStandbyPicker (#23790) into StickyTaskAssignor. Without
rack.aware.assignment.tags, the assignment is unchanged.

Rack diversity ranks above stickiness, so standbys are now assigned in
four steps:

- Steps 1-2 (rack-aware): a previous member whose process is a
candidate, else the least-loaded candidate.
- Steps 3-4 (tag-blind; same as AK 4.2-4.4 releases): a previous member,
else the least-loaded process.

A process has room while one of its members is below the per-member
quota on active plus standby tasks; a least-loaded pick goes to that
member. After each placement, the assignor reports the change to the
picker with updated(), or updatedAll() when the quota drops, since a
lower quota can take the room of any process.

StreamsAssignorBenchmark gets a rackAwareTags parameter with five tag
layouts, two of them with one host per process, and standbyReplicas=2.

KAFKA-21396: Report active task restore progress the broker acts on (#23987)

A client reports the changelog offsets of an active task only while it
restores the task. The heartbeat carries offsets only when the
assignment changes, when streams.task.offset.interval.ms passes (default
60 sec), or when a warm-up task is within acceptable.recovery.lag. So
the broker learned that an active task had finished restoring, or had come
within acceptable.recovery.lag, only with the next periodic report.
Until then the refiner took the owner to be restoring the task with an
old lag. It did not protect the owner as hot, and it granted a migration
off that owner cold instead of staging it behind a warm-up task.

The client now also sends offsets on the next heartbeat when an active
task it restores comes within acceptable.recovery.lag, when an  active
task that was in the last sent offsets has dropped out of them,  ie,
finished restoring, and when an active task starts to restore, ie,
RUNNING  to RESTORING transition after a local TaskCorruptedException.

The refiner can still run on another member's heartbeat before the
member that finished restoring has sent its offsets. That window is now
at most one heartbeat interval, instead of the task offset interval.

MINOR: Update the consumer and streams group state without scanning all members (#24153)

`ConsumerGroup` and `StreamsGroup` check every member on each member
update, member removal and epoch change (and topology change for
streams) to decide whether the group is `RECONCILING` or `STABLE`.
Updating the members of a group one at a time, for instance when loading
a group or converting a classic group, makes this O(N^2) for a group of
N members.

This patch keeps the number of stable members at each member epoch in a
`TimelineHashMap`, which `updateMember` and `removeMember` adjust for
the old and the new member. The group is reconciling when the count at
the target assignment epoch is below the number of members, so the
counts do not depend on the assignment epoch and stay valid in any
replay order.

Median time per operation for a stable consumer group of N members
subscribed to 5 topics of 16 partitions, before -> after (JMH). Load
replays the group records, conversion is
`ConsumerGroup#fromClassicGroup`, and heartbeat moves one member between
`STABLE` and `UNREVOKED_PARTITIONS`.

|------|-------------------|-------------------|--------------------| |

KAFKA-21448: Fix quadratic resize of ImplicitLinkedHashCollection (#24183)

Since 598caf0864 (MINOR: Make the message array length limit
configurable), Java CI builds that run the `clients` tests have been
hitting the 210-minute timeout, on PRs and on trunk. That commit adds
`testArrayLengthAboveDefaultMaxIsAcceptedWhenRaised` to
`SimpleArraysMessageTest`, which reads an array of 1,000,001 entries
keyed by consecutive `int32` values. The test runs for 2h19m to 2h52m in
the main CI test job, and for about 25 minutes when it runs with few
other tests.

The time goes into `ImplicitLinkedHashCollection.changeCapacity`. It
removes each element from the old array before inserting it into the new
one, and each removal reseats every element up to the next empty slot,
so a resize is quadratic when the hash codes form long probe runs.
Generated keyed collections with an `int32` map key hash to the key
itself, so consecutive keys fill a single run. Adding 100,000
consecutive keys to a collection presized for 1,000, as generated
readers do, takes about 17 seconds. The resize has worked this way since
the class was added; the new test is the first to read such a large
array.

This patch copies the elements into the new array in insertion order
and drops the old array without removing anything from it. The new
array and links are the same as before. Adding 100,000 and 1,000,001
consecutive keys now takes about 5 ms and 14 ms, and the test about
60 ms locally.

KAFKA-20731: transitToUpdateStandby is called without checking ACTIVE_RESTORING (#22864)

`DefaultStateUpdater` could call the non-idempotent
`ChangelogReader#transitToUpdateStandby` method while the changelog
reader was already in `STANDBY_UPDATING`. This could happen after all
updating standby tasks were paused or removed because the empty-task
state did not transition the reader back to `ACTIVE_RESTORING`. Adding
or resuming a standby task afterward attempted the standby transition
again, throwing an `IllegalStateException` and terminating the state
updater thread.

- When there are no updating tasks, the reader is in `ACTIVE_RESTORING`.

pauses, removals, failures, and active restoration completion so that
the reader state remains consistent with the updating task set.

covers standby pause, removal, failure, and resume sequences.

KAFKA-21458, KAFKA-21431: Update target assignment on classic heartbeats to consumer groups (#24108)

Unlike consumer heartbeats, classic heartbeats to a consumer group
neither refresh the subscription metadata nor compute the target
assignment. When all the members of a consumer group use the classic
protocol, nothing does. This causes two bugs:

* KAFKA-21431: In such a group, a group epoch bump does not lead to a
  new target assignment until a member rejoins. Since KAFKA-20272,
  classic members are only told to rejoin once a newer target
  assignment is available, so the group stays on its stale assignment.
  This happens when the last member using the consumer protocol leaves
  a group that cannot be downgraded, or when assignment batching or
  offload defers the computation.

* KAFKA-21458: When all the members use the classic protocol, topic
  creations and partition increases do not bump the group epoch until a
  member rejoins. In a classic group, the leader would detect them and
  rejoin, but classic members of a consumer group have no leader.

Make classic heartbeats refresh the subscription metadata when it has
expired and update the target assignment, like consumer heartbeats do.

KAFKA-21372: Build the PartitionGroup#readyToProcess log message lazily (#23985)

### The issue
`PartitionGroup#readyToProcess` formats a not-ready message on every
call and `StreamTask` runs it per record. `StreamTask` logs that message
at most once every 120s and discards the rest. Tasks that read a busy
topic together with a quiet one pay this cost on almost every record.

### Why it happened
KAFKA-19682 (#20693) replaced parameterized `logger.trace` calls with
eager `String.format` calls collected in a `StringBuilder`.
`StreamTask#isProcessable` also resolved the message before
`maybeLogNotReady` checked the log interval.

### The fix
- `ReadyToProcessResult` holds a `Supplier<String>`. `maybeLogNotReady`
calls it only when it logs.
- The suppliers capture only immutable locals, so they are safe with
`SynchronizedPartitionGroup`.
- The message for the partition that blocks processing is unchanged.
When no partition has data, the message now lists the partitions past
their idle deadline. Before, it printed a "fetched lag" line for each of
them.

### Tests
- New
`PartitionGroupTest#shouldNotFormatNotReadyLogMessageUntilRequested`. It
fails on trunk and passes with the fix.
- `PartitionGroupTest`, `StreamTaskTest` and
`SynchronizedPartitionGroupTest` pass unchanged.
- Microbenchmark with two partitions, one of them idle: 1435 → 85 ns and
3288 → 264 B per call while waiting; 1904 → 214 ns and 1128 → 344 B once
the idle deadline has passed.

KAFKA-21230: Build RocksDB WriteBatch at commit (#23999)

`RocksDBTransactionBuffer` writes every staged write twice: to
`pendingWrites` on the heap, which serves reads, and to a native RocksDB
`WriteBatch`. The `WriteBatch` holds native memory for the whole
transaction, and the buffer changes it while it holds the write lock.

The buffer now stages writes on the heap only. Writes to other column
families and range deletes also stay on the heap until the commit. At
commit, `prepareFlush()` builds the `WriteBatch` from the staged state
outside the write lock, and `flushToBase()` writes it to RocksDB under
the write lock. A JMH model of the two designs measured writes 2 to 7
times faster, and commits 8 to 12 times faster when the transaction
overwrites keys. A commit with no overwrites and 1000-byte values is up
to 28% slower.

Because no buffer writes to a backend at stage time now, the
`stageToBackend` hook of `AbstractTransactionBuffer` has no function.
This change removes it and all of its implementations.

The uncommitted-bytes estimate also counted a key once for each write in
a transaction, so a key written many times could cause an early commit
with little staged data. `AbstractTransactionBuffer.stage` now subtracts
the size of the previous entry for the key before it adds the new entry.
`RocksDBTransactionBuffer` uses this shared accounting for all of its
staged data.

`statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes` now counts each staged write once.
Before, it counted the heap copy and the `WriteBatch` copy. The commit
still needs a native `WriteBatch`, but only for one store at a time,
because stores commit one after the other. The extra memory at commit is
therefore at most the uncommitted bytes of the largest store. A thread
now commits early when its uncommitted bytes plus the uncommitted bytes
of its largest store exceed its share of the limit. The global thread
uses the same check. The limit is thus again a bound on the memory at
commit.

KAFKA-21033: Back off once per round when creating Streams internal topics (#23363)

The KAFKA-10357 refactoring (#20326) extracted the internal-topic
creation loop of  `InternalTopicManager.makeReady` into a `createTopics`
helper and carried the end-of-round  backoff block into the per-topic
result loop. Since 4.3.0, after every successfully  created topic, the
manager logs "Topics ... could not be made ready" and sleeps
`retry.backoff.ms` when other topics of the same batch are not yet
iterated. The first  initialization of a topology with N internal topics
pays ~(N-1) * retry.backoff.ms of  sleep even when every create succeeds
immediately: with the 100 ms default, a topology  with 168 internal
topics loses ~17 seconds before its first rebalance completes, plus one
spurious INFO line per topic. The misplaced block also checked the
deadline mid-round, so  `makeReady` could throw `TimeoutException` while
the remaining futures of the round had  already succeeded, and the INFO
line listed not-yet-iterated topics as "could not be made  ready".

The refactor also dropped the backoff for rounds that create nothing:
when a topic is  marked for deletion or a describe transiently fails,
`tempUnknownTopics` is non-empty  while `topicsToCreate` is empty, and
`makeReady` re-describes in a hot loop until the  deadline (by default
`max.poll.interval.ms / 2`).

Move the backoff to the end of `makeReady`'s round, next to its existing
deadline check,  through the `maybeSleep` helper the file already uses
for setup and validation rounds.  This restores the pre-4.3 semantics:
one backoff per round, covering both the create path  and the
unknown-topics path. The retry log line now reads "Internal topics ...
could not  be made ready", consistent with the other rounds.
`maybeSleep` switches from `Utils.sleep`  to `time.sleep` so more
backoff calls in the file are observable with `MockTime`, and the
now-unused  deadline parameter of `createTopics` is dropped.

KAFKA-21410: Do not seed aborted transactions that ended before the cleaning start (#24072)

When a cleaning pass fills its offset map, it stops in the middle of a
segment and the next pass starts at that offset. `buildOffsetMap` seeds
`CleanedTransactionMetadata` with `log.collectAbortedTransactions(start,
end)`, but `LocalLog.collectAbortedTransactions` used the log start
offset as the lower bound of the transaction index search, so it also
returned aborted transactions of that segment that ended before
`start`. The pass begins reading at the offset index entry at or below
`start` and may never see their ABORT markers. Every later
transactional batch of such a producer, including committed ones, is
then treated as aborted and its keys are left out of the offset map. A
committed tombstone is ignored: the older value of the key is kept, the
tombstone is removed after `delete.retention.ms`, and the deleted key
comes back (KAFKA-21410).

`LocalLog.collectAbortedTransactions` now uses the start offset both to
find the first segment and as the lower bound, as the fetch path does,
and no longer takes the log start offset. `cleanSegments` passes the
base offset of each segment it rewrites, and an aborted transaction is
indexed in the segment that holds its ABORT marker, so it still gets
the full segment range it needs to rebuild the transaction index
(KAFKA-13727). For a segment that starts below the log start offset,
aborted transactions whose ABORT marker is below the log start offset
used to be skipped, so their data was kept as if committed and their
index entries were dropped; now they are collected like the rest of
the segment. All of it is below the log start offset, where no fetch
reads.

KAFKA-21317: Continue timestamp search across local and remote log segments (#24028)

After `DeleteRecords` advances the log start offset into a segment, that
segment's cached maximum timestamp can belong to a record below the new
start offset. A lookup in that segment can return empty even though a
later segment contains a valid match. Both local and tiered timestamp
searches can stop too early in this case.

This PR fixes both paths:

- Continue `UnifiedLog.searchOffsetInLocalLog` after an empty segment
lookup, using segment base offsets to skip segments before the starting
offset.
- Continue remote lookups after empty results and track the last
searched offset so segments spanning multiple leader epochs are not
fetched again.
- Reuse the local lookup from `RemoteLogManager`, passing the same
segment snapshot used for the coverage check, and return its result once
the search reaches local storage.

Regression coverage includes a local segment whose matching record is
below the log start offset, later remote matches within and across
leader epochs, a remote segment spanning multiple epochs, and a single
local search when no record matches, and consistent results when local
retention changes the segment list between the coverage check and
lookup.

KAFKA-20981: fail on an unknown status code in the Streams heartbeat response (#23262)

A new StreamsGroupHeartbeatResponse status code is a semantic contract
change: it requires a KIP and a request-version bump, and the broker
must gate the new code so it is only sent to clients that advertise the
introducing version (as it does today for MISSING_CLIENT_TAGS, withheld
from v0 clients). If a broker bug sends a code an older client does not
recognize, the client decodes every status via Status.fromCode, which
throws -- and that throw, raised while handling the heartbeat response,
is currently swallowed (KAFKA-20860): the client keeps heartbeating,
advances its member epoch, and silently ignores the assignment and every
one after it, while the coordinator sees a healthy member.

This PR rejects the response as a whole, before any of it is applied, if
it carries a status this client cannot interpret: log it, surface a
KafkaException through the uncaught-exception handler, and fail the
member, so the error is visible instead of silently dropping every
assignment.

heartbeat.

KAFKA-21370: Return STREAMS_INVALID_TOPOLOGY_EPOCH for topology epoch mismatches (#23978)

KIP-1071 defines STREAMS_INVALID_TOPOLOGY_EPOCH for a member that sends
a topology that differs from the group's topology at the same epoch, but
the group coordinator returned INVALID_REQUEST in that case. The streams
group heartbeat now returns STREAMS_INVALID_TOPOLOGY_EPOCH when the
topology differs at the same epoch. When the topology differs at a
higher epoch, it keeps returning INVALID_REQUEST, since topology updates
are not supported yet.

STREAMS_INVALID_TOPOLOGY_EPOCH instead of INVALID_REQUEST when the
pushed epoch does not match the group's current topology epoch, and

KAFKA-21111 [3/N]: Promote the standby of an orphan on a member that cannot report its progress (#23794)

This is the third change of the series that makes the warm-up task
refiner (KAFKA-20665) compatible with clients that speak version 0 of
the streams group heartbeat (see KAFKA-21111), on top of #23784.

A copy of a task on a member that does not report its restore progress
can never be observed to be caught up, so it is neither promoted nor
protected, like any other copy that is not caught up. There is one
exception, for an orphan: a stateful task that nobody holds as an active
task, whose target owner can be warmed up but holds no state for it. If
the target assignment also names the holder of the unobservable copy as
a standby holder of the task, the holder runs the task as temporary
owner while the target owner warms up. A holder that heartbeats with
version 0, or whose version is not known yet, is such a member.

Here the alternative to promoting a copy of unknown lag is a restore
from scratch on the target owner next to a standby task that would have
to restore anyway, whereas elsewhere the alternative is keeping a
running owner. If the copy turns out to be stale, the temporary owner
restores it as an active task before it processes anything, which is the
restore the target assignment demands of it as a standby holder anyway.
If it is close, the task resumes processing at once. The hand-over then
demotes the temporary owner to its standby task in place.

The refiner is not the default yet, so this change is not live. The
tests cover the promotion for a holder of version 0 and for one of
unknown version, and the cases where it must not apply: a holder that
reports being behind, a standby that the target assignment does not keep
on its holder, and a target owner that cannot be warmed up.

KAFKA-21341: Report a TLS close_notify without a TCP FIN as a disconnect (#23933)

When a TLS `close_notify` arrives in the same read as application data,
`SslTransportLayer.read` returns the data and leaves the close for a
later read, but `updateBytesBuffered` clears `hasBytesBuffered`, so the
Selector never reads the channel again unless a TCP FIN arrives. A peer
may close only its TLS write side and keep the TCP connection open (RFC
8446 section 6.1, e.g. a TLS-terminating proxy), and a request on that
connection then waits for `request.timeout.ms`.

`hasBytesBuffered()` now also returns true once the engine's inbound
side is done, so the Selector reads the channel again, and that read
throws `EOFException` once no decrypted data is left. The disconnect is
reported at once, as it already is when `close_notify` arrives without
data. A read into a full buffer, such as the payload of a zero-length
frame, still returns 0, and a scattering read returns the bytes it has
already read instead of losing them to that exception.

KAFKA-21230: Pause task executors on byte limit (#23984)

#23728 pauses processing and punctuation while the uncommitted state
store bytes of a StreamThread exceed `statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes`.
That pause is in `runOnceWithoutProcessingThreads`. When processing
threads are enabled, task executors process records and run punctuators
independently of the StreamThread loop, so the pause does not stop them.
If a commit is skipped during a rebalance, or fails, the executors
continue to write to the state stores. The uncommitted bytes then
increase without bound, and the native memory of the transaction buffers
increases with them.

`StreamThread#maybePauseProcessingForUncommittedBytes()` now also sets
the pause on the processing threads, through the new
`TaskManager#setProcessingThreadsPaused`. `runOnceWithProcessingThreads`
calls it after `maybeCommit`. The scheduling `TaskManager` gains
`setProcessingPaused` and `processingPaused`.

`DefaultTaskManager` keeps the flag in a volatile field for each
StreamThread. It does not use `TaskExecutionMetadata`, because all
StreamThreads share that object. While the flag is set, `canProgress`
returns false, so `assignNextTask` assigns no task and
`awaitProcessableTasks` blocks. When processing resumes,
`DefaultTaskManager` signals the executors. While paused,
`DefaultTaskExecutor` does not process or punctuate its current task.
The task makes no progress, so the executor releases it through the
existing path for such tasks.

`GlobalStreamThread` does not need this change. One thread writes,
checks and flushes synchronously, and no condition skips the flush.

Both tests in `UncommittedBytesLimitIntegrationTest` now also run with
processing threads enabled.

KAFKA-21214: [8/8] Add the uniform2 consumer group assignor (#23723)

The uniform assignor balances the total number of partitions per member
but not the partitions of each topic: with homogeneous subscriptions, a
member can get all the partitions of a topic while the others get none
of them. The throughput is usually about the same across the partitions
of a topic but not across topics, so adding members does not spread the
load.

This patch adds uniform2, the next version of the uniform assignor, from
the steps of the previous patches. It lives next to the uniform assignor
while it is developed and is not registered as a built-in assignor. Its
assignments have these properties, in priority order:
- Every partition of every subscribed topic goes to exactly one of its
  subscribers.
- Every subscriber of a topic gets the same number of its partitions,
  the minimum quota, or one more, with an extra partition.
- No extra partition could move to another subscriber of its topic
  whose assignment is at least two partitions smaller.
- Partitions stay with their owners where the above allows. The
  placement moves the fewest partitions for the quotas, and an
  assignment that already has these properties is returned unchanged.
- The result is deterministic.

  runs the `KeepStickyExtraPartitions`, `AssignRemainingExtraPartitions`

When a broker becomes the leader of a `__transaction_state` partition,
`TransactionStateManager` loads the log up to the log end offset. A
newly elected leader can have records above the high watermark that are
not committed yet and can still be truncated if leadership moves again,
even with clean elections. The coordinator then acts on state that is
later rolled back. For example, it can send COMMIT markers for a

would miss committed records.

the load once the high watermark reaches the log end offset. The high

listener.

KAFKA-21344: Handle partition rotation for share fetches (#23951)

A share fetch hands its record budget to partitions in the order they
are read, so the partition read first  takes the largest share. Two
things decided that order earlier and together they could starve a
partition, hence changed the behaviour.

Earlier:
- `SharePartitionManager` rotated the fetch list by `sessionEpoch %
size`. The client bumps the epoch on both
  ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge, so in a poll-and-commit loop fetch
epochs step by two and the rotation is
  constant. One unpaired request flips the parity, and with two
partitions the rotation then undoes the
  session reorder on every fetch, so the same partition is read first
until the other starves.
- `ShareSessionContext` moved served partitions to the end of the
session from inside the response iterator,
  in the iteration order of the response map. That map had passed
through `HashMap` copies, so when every
  partition returned records the session ended up in hash order and the
same partition led every fetch.

PR:

This change removes the epoch rotation from the fetch path and makes the
session reorder deterministic from  the fetch order. The fetch order is
preserved through `ShareFetchUtils`, `ShareFetch` and `KafkaApis` with
`LinkedHashMap`s. `ShareSessionContext` reorders the session in one pass

KAFKA-21234: FileRecords#readInto should honor slice boundaries (#23737)

When the metadata layer (e.g. MetadataLoader) tries to read a slice of
records from KRaft which is greater than
KafkaRaftClient#MAX_BATCH_SIZE_BYTES, the RecordsIterator can return
records which are past the slice (HWM). As it iterates through this
slice of
records, FileRecords#readInto reads from disk the minimum of the bytes
until end of the file and the remaining space in the associated buffer.
In the case of the former, this can lead to a metadata error where the
node tries to snapshot with records past the HWM.

For the metadata error to occur, the following three pre-conditions must
be met:

1. One committed read handed to a listener is larger than 8 MiB.
2. The segment file has bytes after the HWM, meaning records this node
already appended but that aren't committed yet.
3. For the error to actually show up, the snapshot generator emits a
snapshot from the resulting image before the HWM catches up.

The underlying cause is the same as KAFKA-20841. Thanks to @[person]
for working on this issue as part of
https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/22963.

Change `FileRecords#readInto` which reads from the underlying file to
the minimum of:

1. The remaining space in the associated buffer, which in the case of
RecordsIterator is the minimum of the FileRecords' record size and
the batch size defined by KRaft.
2. The end byte position of the FileRecords object, rather than the end
of the underlying file. This ensures when a caller constructs a
FileRecords slice of [start position, HWM), no bytes past the HWM are
read into memory.

KAFKA-21280: Do not send stale bytes after a failed file read in SslTransportLayer.transferFrom (#23832)

`SslTransportLayer.transferFrom` clears `fileChannelBuffer` before
reading the next chunk of the file. When the read threw, or returned no
bytes, the buffer was left cleared rather than flipped, so it still
looked full of the previous chunk. If bytes had already been written in
the same call the `IOException` was swallowed, and the next call sent
the stale buffer as the contents of the position that could not be read:

change;

With transaction V2, an EndTxn(COMMIT) at the current epoch on a
transaction
in Empty, CompleteCommit or CompleteAbort state returned
INVALID_TXN_STATE,
which is fatal to the client. A coordinator that has lost leadership but
not
yet applied the metadata change sees the transaction in exactly this
state,

from its
stale cache.

handled:

up

the

the

NONE and
CompleteAbort + Commit + Retry still returns PRODUCER_FENCED.

KAFKA-20999: [1/N] Add RackAwareStandbyPicker for rack-aware standby placement (#23790)

First part of rack-aware standby placement for streams groups. It adds
RackAwareStandbyPicker, which the sticky assignor and balanced assignor
will use to place standbys by rack.aware.assignment.tags. Nothing calls
it yet; the next PR wires it into StickyTaskAssignor.

A process meets a tag key when it has a value for it that no holder of
the task has yet. For the next standby of a task, pick() chooses the
conditions: every tag key with an unused value if a process with room
meets them all; otherwise, the tag keys in configured order, each kept
only if a process with room still meets it together with those kept so
far. It returns the conditions together with the least-loaded process
with room that meets them, or null once no process with room can make
the task more diverse.

The processes sit in a tree with one level per tag key, so a pick does
not scan every combination of tag values. Each node keeps the
least-loaded process with room below it, and its children are ordered by
it. The caller reports load and room changes with updated() and
updatedAll(), which repair only the affected paths.

KAFKA-14302: Advance restored offsets after changelog catch-up (#23298)

## What is the bug?

When restoring an empty changelog with a non-zero end offset,
ProcessorStateManager does not update the restored offset because no
records are applied.

As a result, changelogOffsets() can report 0 even though restoration has
completed at a higher offset. This can cause Kafka Streams to
incorrectly report recovery lag for the task.

## What does this change do?

The fix advances the restored offset once changelog restoration has
actually reached its known boundary.

The implementation preserves the existing offset semantics and ensures
that the restored offset does not move backwards.

## Testing

Added regression coverage for:

* An empty changelog with a high end offset.
* Task lag calculation after changelog restoration.
* Active and standby restore scenarios.

Existing relevant Streams tests also pass.

KAFKA-21253: Always clear record collector offsets in closeDirty (#23791)

`RecordCollectorImpl.closeDirty()` aborts the open transaction before
calling `close()`, which clears the collector's changelog offsets. If
the abort throws, `close()` is skipped and the offsets are kept. This
happens with an `IllegalStateException` after a timed-out
`commitTransaction()`. The revived task reuses the collector, so if it
is closed clean while its wiped store is still restoring, those stale
offsets are checkpointed. The next restore then skips the missing
records.

This change moves `close()` into a `finally` block so the offsets are
always cleared. It also logs the abort failure at ERROR before
rethrowing. The caller still swallows the exception, and before this
change it was only logged at DEBUG, without the exception.

`CommitTimeoutDirtyCloseIntegrationTest` uses the fault proxy to
reproduce this. A delayed EndTxn leaves a commit pending, so the abort
fails. A later `ILLEGAL_GENERATION` on `TxnOffsetCommit` migrates the
thread, and the restoring task is closed clean.

The associated integration test replicates the issue and without the fix
in this PR it fails.

KAFKA-21111 [2/N]: Grant tasks at once to members that cannot be warmed up (#23784)

This is the second change of the series that makes the warm-up task
refiner (KAFKA-20665) compatible with clients that speak version 0 of
the streams group heartbeat (see KAFKA-21111), on top of #23761.

A warm-up task can only complete a migration if the coordinator observes
the target owner restoring it, which a member that heartbeats with
version 0 never allows, as it does not report task offsets. When the
target assignment moves a stateful task to such a member, the refiner no
longer stages the migration. It lets the target assignment through for
that task, so the current owner revokes it and the target owner takes it
over, as it would without a refiner.

The check sits after the readiness check, so that a move between two
members of one process still happens inside the instance, and before the
analysis of the incumbent and of the copies, so that a caught-up copy on
another process is not promoted as a temporary owner. That detour would
only postpone the same cold grant and add a second hand-over. The
version of the current owner is irrelevant: a member that processes a
task is hot by definition, and keeps it while a target owner that can be
warmed up restores it. If the target owner already holds a standby task
of the task, the client recycles it into the active task, so the grant
is warm in the common case, even though the coordinator cannot see that.

The refiner is not the default yet, so this change is not live. The
tests cover the grant, the missing detour through a caught-up copy, and
a current owner of version 0 that keeps its task.

KAFKA-21214: [3/N] Add the quotas and the first two steps of the uniform2 assignor (#23733)

uniform2 decides how many partitions of every topic each member gets,
its quotas, in three steps, and then places the partitions. A topic with
P partitions and N subscribers has a minimum quota of P / N partitions,
and its P % N extra partitions go to as many distinct subscribers.

This patch adds the quotas and their first two steps:
- `Quotas` holds the minimum quota and the extra partitions of every
  topic, the members getting the extra partitions, and the assignment
  sizes of the members. The steps give the extra partitions and move
  them.
- `KeepStickyExtraPartitions`: a member owning more than the minimum
  quota of a topic keeps one of its extra partitions, the members with
  the smallest assignments first when the owners outnumber the extra
  partitions.
- `AssignRemainingExtraPartitions` gives the extra partitions that
  nobody kept, one at a time, to subscribers without one of the topic,
  among the ones with the smallest assignments: the topics with the
  fewest subscribers first, and round robin within a cohort. It returns
  without allocating anything when the owners kept them all.
- `IntPair` packs two ints in a long, so that pairs sort in a `long[]`
  or a `LongHeap` without allocating.
- A step is created with what it works on and run once; the assignor
  runs the steps in order in a later patch.
- `QuotasFixture` holds the indexed group, the current assignment and
  the quotas of a group for the tests of the steps.

The balance step comes in a later patch.

KAFKA-21194 [1/N]: Place active tasks with the Sainte-Laguë method in the balanced assignor (#23755)

The balanced task assignor placed stateful active tasks round-robin over
the processes and then ran a fix-up loop that moves tasks between
processes while a move reduces the skew of the per-member load. Every
pass of that loop tests all pairs of processes, so it costs O(P^2) per
pass even when nothing moves.

This deals the active tasks with the Sainte-Laguë divisor method
instead: in sorted task order, each task goes to the process with the
smallest (2n + 1) / c, where n is the number of tasks the process holds
so far and c its number of members, ties going to the smaller process
ID. Stateless tasks continue the same sequence after the stateful ones,

coordinator retained the previous rack ID. During static member

KAFKA-21111 [1/N]: Tell the refiner which members may be given a warm-up task (#23761)

This is the first change of a series that makes the warm-up task refiner
(KAFKA-20665) compatible with clients that speak version 0 of the
streams group heartbeat (4.2 and 4.3), and with a coordinator failover
during which the coordinator does not know the version of any member. A
warm-up task is only useful if the coordinator can observe how far its
holder has restored it, which a member reports through the task offsets
of a version 1 heartbeat. A version 0 member never does, so it could
never be promoted from warm-up to active.

This change only provides the information, and nothing uses it yet. The
coordinator records the version of every member's last heartbeat as
transient state of the streams group, with the same lifecycle as the
reported task offsets: written in the heartbeat path, dropped when the
member is removed, and not known again after a coordinator failover
until the member heartbeats. It is deliberately not persisted, so that
it can never outlive the client that sent it. The refiner is handed an
immutable view of it, and decides itself which versions it can warm up.
A member that is missing from the map, because the coordinator has not
heard from the member since it loaded the group, has an unknown version.
The refiner ignores the new input for now; the following changes of this
series use it.

The uniform assignor balances the total number of partitions per member
but not the partitions of each topic: with homogeneous subscriptions, a
member can get all the partitions of a topic while the others get none
of them. uniform2, the next version of the uniform assignor, spreads
every topic over its subscribers. It reads the group, decides how many
partitions of every topic each member gets, its quotas, in three steps,
and then places the partitions. This stack adds it one step at a time,

  subscription into cohorts.
- `CurrentAssignment` reads the owner of every partition. What the
  members hold of topics they do not subscribe to, or which no longer
  exist, is stale and dropped.

KAFKA-21196: Release memory held by cancelled CoordinatorExecutorImpl tasks (#23674)

When a `CoordinatorExecutorImpl` task is cancelled, it remains in the
executor queue or in the event processor queue until it is processed and
it retains its runnable, its operation and the result of its runnable in
the meantime. When the group coordinator is overloaded, these queues can
grow large and retain data structures that are no longer needed, e.g.
the metadata image captured by the regular expression resolution.

This patch boxes the runnable, the operation and the result in a `Task`
object which releases them when the task is cancelled. The operation and
the result are also released once the operation is executed because the
write event is retained until its records are committed.

KAFKA-20998: Add balanced task assignor for streams groups (#23419)

The streams rebalance protocol (KIP-1071) ships one built-in task
assignor, "sticky". This adds a second, "balanced", a translation of the
placement in the classic `HighAvailabilityTaskAssignor`:

- Stateful active tasks are dealt round-robin over the processes, then
  moved between processes while a move reduces the per-member load skew.
- Standbys go to the least loaded process that does not hold the task,
  and stateless tasks fill in by active task load.
- Within a process, tasks are spread over its members the way the
  classic client spreads them over its stream threads
  (`assignTasksToThreads`): stateful actives, then standbys, then
  stateless actives, each round levelling the members' task counts. A
  stateful task stays on the member that holds it in any role (active,
  standby or warm-up) where that leaves no other member short.

Reported offsets are not read: warm-up tasks are the assignment
refiner's job (KAFKA-20665), and rack-aware standby placement is
KAFKA-20999. A shortfall of standby replicas is logged once per

KAFKA-20803: Demultiplex batched persister responses once (WriteStateHandler) (#22835)

fix: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20803

PersisterStateManager coalesces many partitions into a single
WRITE_SHARE_GROUP_STATE RPC. On completion, every per-partition handler
re-scanned the full combined response to find its own slice — N handlers
*  O(N) scan = O(N ^ 2 ), all on the single send thread, stalling the
send loop.

This PR demultiplexes the combined response once into a topicId ->
partition -> result index (PartitionResultIndex, built in the send loop
and shared across the handlers of one coalesced request) and  converts
WriteStateHandler to an O(1) lookup.

Scope is deliberately limited to WRITE: it is the hot path, since every
acknowledgement/commit drives a write. readState runs once per
SharePartition lifetime, initializeState once per group-topic-partition,
and delete/read-summary are admin-invoked — for those, building an index
would cost more than the lookup it saves, so they keep the existing

KAFKA-21161: Checkpoint consumed offset over produced offset for source-topic changelog stores (#23585)

When a task both consumes a source-topic changelog partition (a KTable
that reuses its  source topic as its changelog) and produces to that
same partition, `StreamTask.checkpointableOffsets()`  gave the produced
offset precedence over the consumed offset. On a clean suspend, close,
or  recycle, the store's changelog offset was set to the last offset the
task *wrote*, which can be  ahead of the last offset actually *applied*
to the store. A later restore or standby update  starting from that
checkpoint silently skips the records in between, leaving those keys
stale or  missing — with no error or warning.

Fix: let `consumedOffsets` win over `recordCollector.offsets()` in
`checkpointableOffsets()`. For a  source-topic changelog the store is
filled by consuming the partition, so the consumed offset is  what was
applied to the store.

This only affects a partition that is both consumed and produced to
*and* is a store changelog —  i.e. a source-topic changelog. Dedicated
changelog, output, and repartition partitions are never in
`consumedOffsets` (only input partitions are), so their produced offsets
are unchanged.

-

`shouldCheckpointConsumedOffsetNotProducedOffsetForSourceChangelogPartition`
— new; fails without the fix.
- `shouldCheckpointProducedOffsetForDedicatedChangelogPartition` — new;
guards that dedicated changelogs keep their produced offset.

`shouldCommitWhileUpdateSnapshotWithTheConsumedOffsetsForSuspendedRunningTask`
— updated; it encoded the old produced-wins behavior.

KAFKA-14405: Log a warning when users attempt to set a config controlled by Streams (#22586)

Kafka Streams assigns some of the underlying consumer and producer
configs itself and silently ignored a user-supplied value for them, so
there was no way to tell that the setting had no effect. Two unrelated
mechanisms did this: a checker driven by the `NON_CONFIGURABLE_*` arrays
that inspected the prefix-extracted user properties, and direct `put()`
calls applied after those properties were merged, which warned about
nothing at all.

Replace both with a single helper, `overwriteControlledConfig`, applied
to  the fully assembled config map so that an override is caught in one
place whichever prefix supplied it, and split the config sets by intent:
`DEFAULT_*` holds defaults the user may still override, `CONTROLLED_*`
holds  values the user cannot. The `_EOS_ONLY` maps carry only what
exactly-once  adds and are applied on top of their counterparts.

This closes two gaps. `group.id` and `partition.assignment.strategy` are
documented as controlled by Streams but produced no log line, because
both are forced with a put() after the merge. The per-client prefixes
were only checked against the non-exactly-once set, so
`restore.consumer.isolation.level=read_uncommitted` gave a restore
consumer reading uncommitted records under exactly-once; it now yields
`read_committed`.

Warnings are now all logged at `WARN`, where the non-exactly-once set
was  previously logged at `ERROR`, and a config that is only controlled
under  exactly-once names the processing guarantee as the reason.

A value that differs from the Streams value only in type, such as
`Boolean.FALSE` where Streams sets `"false"`, no longer warns that it is
being replaced by an identical value.
`max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` is a producer config and is now
validated only there, so a value supplied under a consumer prefix is no
longer rejected.

MINOR: Write the streams topology tombstone before the group epoch tombstone (#23552)

Deleting a streams group leaks its topics in the group coordinator's
topic-to-groups index (`groupsByTopics`), which `onMetadataUpdate` uses
to tell groups that a topic they depend on changed.

A streams group's entry in that index is derived from its topology:
replaying a `StreamsGroupTopologyValue` record subscribes the group to
the topology's required topics and replaying its tombstone unsubscribes
it. `StreamsGroup.createGroupTombstoneRecords` wrote the
`StreamsGroupMetadataValue` tombstone before the
`StreamsGroupTopologyValue` tombstone. On replay, the first one removes
the group, so the second one finds no group and returns before
unsubscribing anything. The entry survives for the lifetime of the
coordinator, and every deleted streams group adds to it. The consumer of
the index checks that the group still exists, so the effect is bounded
growth of the index and a spurious metadata refresh request on a group
that later reuses the id, not a failure.

This change writes the topology tombstone before the group epoch
tombstone. This restores the invariant the other group types already
have: every sibling record is torn down before the epoch tombstone, so
the epoch tombstone is the last record of a deletion. Deletions already
in the log with the previous order keep leaking on replay until
compaction removes their tombstones.

The new test builds a streams group with a topology, replays exactly the
records that `createGroupTombstoneRecords` produces, and verifies that
the group is removed and that the index no longer references it. It
fails with the previous record order.

MINOR: Fix static members being fenced by their own instance id (#23542)

A static member that joins with epoch 0 while the coordinator still
considers it active gets UNRELEASED_INSTANCE_ID, which is fatal for the
Java client. This happens when the response to its join is lost or after
a FENCED_MEMBER_EPOCH error, because the client keeps its member id and
rejoins with it. A dynamic member in the same situation simply gets its
assignment back.

The root cause is that the coordinator does not enforce that a member id
keeps its instance id. On a join, a known member id may come with any
instance id, so the coordinator cannot tell that the same member is back
and treats it as a replacement of the instance id's owner, itself.

This patch rejects a join that changes the instance id of an existing
member with INVALID_REQUEST. A known member id on a join is then always
the static member owning the instance id, and it is handled in place:
after a leave with epoch -2 its epoch is reset and it is reconciled,
otherwise it gets its current state back like a dynamic member. This
also removes the tombstone-and-rewrite of a member rejoining with its
own id after leaving. Consumer and streams groups are updated alike.

Tests cover every join case for both protocols.

MINOR: Moving to atomic update of share sessions on initial epoch (#23510)

ShareSessionCache `.remove` and `.maybeCreateSession` are each
individually synchronized — but as two separate calls, not one atomic
unit. If two connections sent an INITIAL_EPOCH request for the same
(groupId, memberId), *faulty client*, at nearly the same time then both
proceed to create a session. `maybeCreateSession` increments
numMembersPerGroup and numPartitions every time it's called. The
sessions map only ever holds one entry per key (second write overwrites
the first), but the counters had already been bumped twice.

on disconnect, only the connection whose mapping still pointed at a live
session gets to decrement the counters. So numMembersPerGroup for that
group gets stuck above zero forever, which means onGroupEmpty never
fires.

KAFKA-21074: Kafka protocol fault proxy clients fixtures (#23438)

A lightweight Kafka wire-protocol fault-injection proxy for integration
tests. Sit it in front of an EmbeddedKafkaCluster, point any client’s
bootstrap.servers at it, and it can inject error codes, drop
connections, or blackhole a client — decoding/encoding with Kafka’s own
protocol classes so it is correct across every wire version (including
flexible/tagged-field ones), no hand-rolled byte offsets.

Placed in `clients/src/testFixtures` so it is reusable from any module.
This is internal test infrastructure only so it does not require a KIP.

Fault primitives, each armed with a fluent, deterministic trigger:

`injectError(apiKey, Errors)` — stamp an error code onto the matching
response,    re-serialized at the correct wire version. Supported APIs:
`END_TXN`,    `INIT_PRODUCER_ID`, `ADD_OFFSETS_TO_TXN`,
`TXN_OFFSET_COMMIT`, `PRODUCE`, `FETCH`    (extensible by registering a
per-API setter).  `disconnectOn(apiKey)` — drop the connection when the
matching response would return    (models the EOS "commit gap"). Works
on any API.  `delayOn(apiKey, Duration)` — hold back the matching
response to model a slow broker,    isolated to that one connection.
`blackholeClient(clientIdSubstring)` — drop all requests from a targeted
client before    the broker sees them, so the broker evicts it by
session timeout (a reversible,    ungraceful one-node partition). Shared
trigger DSL (`Occurrence`): `once()`, `onCall`, `times`, `everyTime()`,
`withProbability(p)`. The deterministic triggers are safe for
assertions; probability is  chaos-mode only. The proxy never closes
sockets unless a `disconnectOn(...)` rule fires,  so it is not itself a
source of flakiness. Rules can be armed/disarmed live from the test
thread and each returns a handle exposing match/fire counts.

`RemoteDeleteLagSegments` / `RemoteDeleteLagBytes` can get latched at a
non-zero value that never drains back to 0 after a partition leader
moves to another broker, even though remote deletion is healthy and no
segment is orphaned in remote storage. It is purely a metrics artifact,
but under frequent leadership movement the broker/cluster aggregate
steps up over time as each affected partition contributes a stuck
residual, producing false-positive "delete lag stuck" alerts.

JIRA: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21098

The copy path was hardened for this exact race in KAFKA-16948 (reset lag

## Summary

Since #22327 (4.3.1, "MINOR: Fixed metrics decompression"),
`ClientTelemetryUtils.decompress` throws `TelemetryTooLargeException`
when the decompressed telemetry payload exceeds `telemetry.max.bytes`.
That exception propagates up through
`ClientTelemetryExporterPlugin.exportMetrics` into
`ClientMetricsManager.processPushTelemetryRequest`, where it's caught by
a generic `catch (Throwable)` that always maps to
`Errors.INVALID_RECORD`.

Per KIP-714, `INVALID_RECORD` means "the client's metrics serialization
is broken, stop pushing" — the Java client reacts by setting its push
interval to `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, permanently disabling telemetry for
that client instance until the process restarts. `TELEMETRY_TOO_LARGE`
is the correct, retryable code for this case — it's exactly what the
pre-decompression wire-size check already returns via
`Errors.forException` in `validatePushRequest`, a few lines above in the
same method.

Typical OTLP metrics decompress at 10-25x their compressed size, so any
client sending a payload that's well within the compressed wire limit
can still trip the decompressed-size check and get silently, permanently
cut off. This was observed in production: after upgrading brokers from
4.3.0 to 4.3.1, every Kafka Streams stream-thread consumer's telemetry
stopped in every environment simultaneously.

## Fix

Add `catch (TelemetryTooLargeException)` before the existing `catch
(Throwable)` in `ClientMetricsManager.processPushTelemetryRequest`,
mapping to `Errors.TELEMETRY_TOO_LARGE` instead of
`Errors.INVALID_RECORD`. This mirrors the `catch (ApiException) ->
Errors.forException(exception)` pattern already used for
`validatePushRequest` just above it — no new error-handling shape
introduced. `TelemetryTooLargeException` already extends `ApiException`
and `Errors.TELEMETRY_TOO_LARGE` already exists (introduced with
KIP-714), so this is a two-catch-bloc…

The assignor gets each member's current assignment as input, but only
considers its active and standby tasks when it computes a sticky
assignment; warm-up tasks are ignored. A warm-up task, however, is a
member restoring the state of a task whose active task is being migrated
to it, so ignoring it means that a re-computed assignment can send the
task somewhere else and throw the restore work away.

holds it becomes a candidate for the corresponding active task (and for
its standby task) before the assignment falls back to picking the least
loaded process.

KAFKA-20873: Fix deadlock between removeStreamThread and addStreamThread (#23004)

JIRA: KAFKA-20873

`KafkaStreams.removeStreamThread(long)` used to hold the
`changeThreadCount` monitor while  waiting for the removed thread to
reach DEAD. When the removal target was the same  StreamThread that
concurrently entered the REPLACE_THREAD uncaught-exception handler, its
`replaceStreamThread -> addStreamThread` path blocked on the same lock,
so the target never  reached DEAD and the waiter waited forever.

`removeStreamThread` now signals the shutdown under the lock, waits for
DEAD without holding  it, and re-acquires it for the bookkeeping.
Releasing the lock exposes races between removal,  thread replacement,
and close, resolved by a single rule: whoever wins the atomic transition
to PENDING_SHUTDOWN owns the thread's death and decides its group
membership operation. A  losing REPLACE_THREAD handler does not spawn a
replacement, so a removal is not silently  undone; a losing removal
skips the thread and scans on, returning `Optional.empty()` when nothing
was removed; a later shutdown request (including close) never changes
the operation  the owner chose, and the failure-path LEAVE_GROUP default
equally yields to an  already-initiated shutdown. The bookkeeping also
keeps the store-provider registration of a  live thread that reused the
removed thread's name, and only throws a TimeoutException when  the wait
for DEAD actually timed out.

Unit tests cover the concurrent-removal, lost-shutdown, name-reuse, and
operation-ownership interleavings; an integration test fails a thread
with REPLACE_THREAD  after a removal wins its shutdown and asserts no
replacement is spawned.

KAFKA-20923: Introduce headerVersions into RPC schema definitions (#23317)

Jira: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20923

KIP-1313:

https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/KAFKA/pages/406624038/KIP-1313+Client+instance+ID+in+all+request+headers

KIP-1313 needs each RPC to declare its request and response header
versions  explicitly, rather than deriving them implicitly from body
flexibility, so that a  later header version (v3, carrying the client
instance ID) can be mapped to specific request versions.

This PR:
- Adds an optional `headerVersions` property to the request/response
message schemas
  and declares it, starting at version 0, for every RPC that has valid
versions.
- Teaches the code generator to emit
`requestHeaderVersion`/`responseHeaderVersion` from it, falling back to
the existing implicit derivation when the property is absent.
- Validates `headerVersions` at parse time: the map must start at
version 0 and cover every version in contiguous, non-overlapping ranges
that end open-ended; header versions must not decrease as body versions
increase; every header version must exist in the `RequestHeader` /
`ResponseHeader` schema; and a flexible body version must map to a
flexible header. `ApiVersionsResponse` is pinned to a v0 response header
at every version so older brokers can always parse it (KIP-511).
- Checks in `ApiMessageTypeTest` that every generated header version
exists and is consistent with body flexibility (a flexible body uses a
flexible header), comparing with `>=` so a later flexible header such as
KIP-1313's v3 request
header needs no test change.

KAFKA-20938: Complete stale JoinGroup/SyncGroup future on superseded classic-group request (#23174)

KAFKA-20423: Fix flakiness of testWakeupWithFetchDataAvailable (More) (#23367)

- Previous PR - https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/22364/

The previous PR changed the test to wait until `MockClient` invokes the
completion callback for the fetch response. However, this callback only
registers a completion handler in `pendingCompletion`; it does not
guarantee that the fetch data has already been added to the
`FetchBuffer`.

As a result, the following race condition can still occur:

1. The test worker finishes waiting for `fetchResponseCompleted`, then
verifies the wakeup exception and the position.
2. After the second `consumer.poll(Duration.ZERO)` has passed
coordinator processing, the heartbeat thread removes the handler from
`pendingCompletion`.
3. If the heartbeat thread is descheduled before executing the handler,
the test worker may observe both the completion queue and the
`FetchBuffer` as empty and return an empty result.
4. The heartbeat thread then resumes and adds the fetch data to the
buffer.

This PR changes the wait condition to `fetcher.hasAvailableFetches()`,
ensuring that fetch data that can actually be returned is present in the
buffer before calling `wakeup()`.

This removes the dependency of the subsequent poll's record verification
on the timing of the heartbeat thread's completion processing.

KAFKA-21010 Another busy loop happens if the member is in JOINING state and bootstrap DNS resolution is not finished (#23348)

Follow-up to (#23227).

Before bootstrap DNS resolution completes,
`coordinatorRequestManager.coordinator()` is empty, causing the
coordinator-unknown path in `maximumTimeToWait()` to return
`heartbeatRequestState.heartbeatIntervalMs()`. However, the heartbeat
interval is initialized to 0 and is not updated until the first
heartbeat response is received. As a result, a member in the JOINING
state reports `maximumTimeToWait() == 0`.

Since the application thread's poll timeout is bounded by this value,
both the application and network threads can busy-spin until the
coordinator is discovered.

Returning `retryBackoffMs` aligns with the behavior discussed in #23227.
Until the coordinator is discovered, no heartbeat can be sent, making
this equivalent to the "nothing to send right now, wait for a backoff"
case for which `FetchRequestManager#maximumTimeToWait()` already returns
the retry backoff. Coordinator discovery itself is also paced by the
coordinator manager's backoff.
